I found interpolation to be more readable because the string fits more snugly into the line of code. For example, when writing a string such as "https://example.com/", I find it much more intuitive to have the domain be interpolated inside the string like "https://{domain}/" rather than inserting it with the concatenation like "https://" + domain + "/" and having those nasty plus signs.

In my personal opinion, I found string interpolation to be more readable. This is because the brackets {} bring more attention to the variable name, and the line of pseudocode is not covered by an abundance of plus symbols, which may make reading at a faster pace more difficult.

For example, here are some variables:
name = "Tom"
gpa = "4.0"

A sentence in interpolation: "Hello {name}, congratulations on passing with a {gpa} GPA!"
A sentence in concatenation: "Hello " + name + ", congratulations on passing with a " + gpa + " GPA!"

To me, the sentence in interpolation is easier to read.

I personally found string concatenation to be more readable. This is likely because C++ is the only high-level language I've learned, and am not particularly familiar with the syntax for string interpolation. For example in C++; a = "Hello ", b = "World", cout << a + b;, then the output would be "Hello World". Same for when came to string interpolation, a = "Hello ", b = "World"  {a}{b}, then the output would be the exact same "Hello World". However, the interpolation syntax was confusing as it seemed like putting a space between {a} {b} would implicitly insert a space, even if " " was not at the end of a = "Hello". Although, at the end of the day it's due to my lack of knowledge and application for string interpolation that leads me to say that string concatenation is more readable.

The + was more readable for me, but I think its due to the fact that math has been a constant in my life since the age of 4 years old, so I know what + is meant to do in a variety of different contexts. While {} are new to me from the last 10ish years and even then I wasn't really sure what they were meant to do, I just knew I needed them or the code wouldn't work.

String concatenation is more readable simply because it has less text to parse through. For example, if a = "(1" and b = "0)", then a + b is much easier to read than {a} {b}. However, it also depends on the context a bit. I like the interpolation of f strings in python, especially in an IDE that can color the interpolated section differently than the rest of the string. f"/Users/{user}/Downloads" is easier for me to read than "/Users/" + user + "/Downloads". So, I think if only variables are used, then concatenation is simpler. But if there is a mix of string with variables interspersed, interpolation is easier.

I found interpolation to be more readable because it got rid of unnecessary spaces that clog up my reading when using concatenation. With interpolation, all that separates a pure string from a variable being dereferenced is "{" and "}", whereas with concatenation, it's "' + " and/or " + '".

I found string interpolation more readable than string concatenation because it integrates variable values directly within the string structure. For example, using "Hello, {name}!" is much cleaner and less error-prone than "Hello, " + name + "!". Interpolation reduces the visual clutter of multiple + operators and quotes, especially in longer strings.

Concatenation was most easier because I am used to it. However, interpolation seems like it would make for more readable code in the more meaningful context. What I mean is it was hard to read concatenation when it was just seemingly random letters/numbers, but when it was within the URLs it made a lot more sense (and wasn't separated out by " + ")

I found string concatenation more readable, because I usually interpret anything inside of quotes to be part of the string itself. Interpolation seems to be a little bit more readable than concatenation. With concatenation, having all the strings separated with a plus sign made it confusing to visualize a final resulting string, interpolation on the other hand made it very simple to visualize the result of how a string variable being inserted in another string.

For numbers, I especially found interpolation ("{}") more readable. When using the + symbol, I would often find myself confusing it with addition. For regular strings or when using variable names, I slightly leaned towards concatenation ("+") as being easier to read, partially due to my experience with using this symbol most often in my own code. That being said, the longer the sentence and the more often variable names are used, I leaned more and more towards finding interpolation more readable.

The questions that utilized the + for concatenation and deliberate use of keywords to replace specific portions of a string were easiest to decipher by printing out the created string. The use of { } and quotes within quotes made it harder for someone who does not know the language being used to read the string.
